title: Maglaj Under Siege: The Joint Blockade
sources: ICTY Prlic et al. Trial Judgment (IT-04-74-T)
content:
When the alliance between ARBiH and HVO forces collapsed in the spring of 1993, one of the most immediate and devastating consequences fell upon the Bosniak population of the Bosna River valley in north-central Bosnia. The town of Maglaj and its surrounding pocket, which had been under VRS pressure from the east since the war's opening months, now found itself blockaded from the west as well by HVO forces. What had been a precarious but survivable frontline position became a sealed enclave, trapping tens of thousands of people in a pocket with no overland supply route and no prospect of relief.

The ICTY Prlic et al. Trial Judgment (IT-04-74-T) addressed the Maglaj blockade within its broader findings on the joint HVO-VRS actions that followed the breakdown of the Croat-Bosniak alliance. HVO forces in the region cooperated with VRS units in maintaining the siege, a collaboration that went beyond mere non-aggression to include coordinated military pressure on ARBiH positions. This cooperation was particularly significant because it demonstrated that the HVO-VRS relationship, nominally one of mutual hostility under the Graz Agreement framework, could in practice produce coordinated action against the Bosniak population when local interests aligned.

The conditions inside the Maglaj pocket deteriorated rapidly once the blockade was established. Cut off from overland supply, the enclave's population depended almost entirely on airdrops conducted by US Air Force transport aircraft as part of Operation Provide Promise, the humanitarian airlift that had been running since February 1993. These airdrops were imprecise and insufficient -- pallets of food and medical supplies were scattered across rough terrain, and a significant proportion landed in areas inaccessible to the enclave's inhabitants or outside the pocket entirely. The caloric intake available to Maglaj's population fell well below subsistence levels for extended periods.

Simultaneously, the pocket endured sustained bombardment from VRS artillery positions in the surrounding hills. The town of Maglaj itself, situated in the narrow Bosna valley, was particularly vulnerable to shelling from elevated positions. Civilian casualties accumulated steadily through the summer and autumn of 1993, while the enclave's medical facilities operated without adequate supplies, electricity, or personnel.

The ARBiH garrison defending the pocket -- centered on the 327th Mountain Brigade -- fought under conditions of extreme material deprivation. Ammunition was rationed to a degree that made sustained defensive operations difficult and offensive action impossible. The brigade's effectiveness depended on the terrain, which favored defense, and on the motivation of soldiers defending their own homes and families. These factors proved sufficient to prevent the pocket's collapse, but they could not prevent the grinding attrition of a siege measured in months.

Maglaj's ordeal illustrated a strategic reality that defined 1993 for the Bosnian government: the two-front war. With HVO forces blocking access from the west and VRS forces pressing from the east, the ARBiH was stretched across multiple disconnected theaters, unable to concentrate force or resupply isolated pockets. Each enclave that held out tied down defending troops and consumed political energy, while each that fell represented both a military loss and a humanitarian catastrophe.

The blockade persisted through the winter of 1993-94 and into the following year. Relief came incrementally -- through local ceasefires, occasional convoy access negotiated by UNPROFOR, and the slow evolution of the military situation as the Washington Agreement of March 1994 ended the Croat-Bosniak conflict. For the people of Maglaj, however, the months of complete isolation left scars that no diplomatic agreement could address. The town had survived, but at a cost measured in hunger, cold, untreated wounds, and the particular despair of a community that knew the outside world was aware of its suffering yet unable or unwilling to intervene decisively.
